title: The Half-Life of Purpose
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The author starts from a common surprise: many team members cannot say why their project matters. A clear why drives engagement, speed and quality, but the post's distinctive claim is that the problem is decay, not a weak launch. Purpose stated once gets buried under deadlines and status updates, so better kickoffs do not fix it. The remedy is to renew the why continuously, tying each review milestone back to the strategic outcome. A bolder practice is to ask team members at random to state the purpose in one sentence and workshop weak answers together, which makes the why something the team owns.
points: Many teams lack a working grasp of why their project exists, which depresses effort, speed and quality.
The diagnosis is that purpose fades over time rather than being poorly announced at launch.
Leaders should reconnect every milestone and review to the strategic outcome it serves.
Cold-calling team members for a one-sentence purpose, then refining it as a group, moves ownership of the why from leader to team.
The advantage of strong performers is keeping strategy alive in the minds of those doing the work, not merely having it on paper.
quotes: Sometimes the most basic ideas are overlooked or assumed. No one disputes that a foundational ingredient for successful projects is that those doing the work understand why it has been assigned and why it matters.

Without a clear and compelling “why,” team members don’t work with the same engagement, effort, or enthusiasm they would otherwise bring. Not knowing the why doesn’t just dampen morale. It slows the work down and shows up in the quality of what gets delivered.
The problem is not that leaders fail to make the case for each assignment or project. It’s that the purpose fades over time.

When the team becomes immersed in planning and execution, the purpose of the project quickly disappears from view. Project leaders who are consumed with keeping the work on track seldom remind the team of the ultimate goal or why this initiative is being pursued.

In team meetings, they ask team members at random to explain in one sentence why the project matters and how it connects to the larger strategy. If the answer is off the mark, the group workshops it together, right there, until it is sharp.

It’s a small ritual that shifts the “why” from something the leader hands down to something the team owns and can defend on demand. Ultimately, keeping the “why” fresh is a discipline that resists the pull of just getting things done.
